Create a socket connection

What I am finding is that the batch will not wait for the SPlus command to
be done before continuing to the next line in the batch script. It turns out
this is really an Splus problem, not that of something strange in the batch
script. I notice that others have experienced in the past in this list, but
the workarounds suggested have all been for Unix.

The command I am using is:  Splus  /BATCH  infile  outfile
(I am using S-Plus 2000).

Any suggestions anyone? Thanks in advance.

Ravi.

Subject: [S] Problem with "object.size"

Dear S-Plus users,
I encountered the following problem:
I have written a function in order to analyse time series ( with monthly
data).
The time series are stored in vectors.
When I test the function with time-series no longer than 400 elements (
approximatively ) the programs works fine, but as soon as the length of
the time series I have to analyse is bigger than 400, the calculation is
dumped.

( the following error is reported with a time-series of length 540 )

Error in 1:ll: Cannot allocate 6786304 bytes: options("object.size") is
 5000000: see options help file
Dumped

Is there anything I can do to avoid this problem ?
Where is exactly the problem ? Does it depend on the efficiency of my
function ?
( S-Plus4 on WindowsNT, pentium 266 with 160 Mb. of RAM )

grateful for any help or advise
Stefano

Subject: [S] ASA StatCompSect Student Paper Competition

Statistical Computing Section
                        American Statistical Association
                        Student Paper Competition 2000

The Statistical Computing Section of the ASA is sponsoring a student
paper session on the topic of Statistical Computing at the Joint
Statistical Meetings in 2000.  Students are encouraged to submit a
paper in this area, which might be original methodological research in
statistical computing, some novel computing application in statistics,
or any other suitable contribution (for example, a software related
project).  Four students will be selected to participate in this
session.

Students at all levels (undergraduate, Masters, and Ph.D.) are
encouraged to participate.  To be eligible, an applicant must be a
registered student in the fall of 1999. The applicant must be the
first author of the paper.  The Section will pay all registration fees
for the selected winners, as well as a substantial allowance for
transportation to the meetings and housing (which in most cases covers
these expenses completely).

To be considered for selection in the session, students must submit an
abstract, a six page manuscript, a resume, and a letter of
recommendation from a mentor familiar with their work.  All materials
must be in English.  The manuscript should be single-spaced in a 10
point font with one inch margins (this is consistent with ASA's
Proceedings guidelines).  All figures, tables and references must be
included in the six-page limit. The letter of recommendation must
include a verification of the applicant's student status and, in the
case of joint authorship, should indicate what fraction of the
contribution is attributable to the applicant.  All electronic
submissions of papers should be in Postscript.

All application materials MUST BE RECEIVED by 5:00 PM PST, Wednesday
January 5, 2000 at the address below.  They will be reviewed by the
Statistical Computing Section Student Paper Competition Award
committee.  Selection will be based on a variety of criteria at the
discretion of the selection committee, and will include innovation and
significance of contribution, amongst others.  Award announcements
will be made in late January, 2000. The decision of the selection
committee will be final.

Applicants not selected for inclusion in the session may submit their
abstract and a registration fee to ASA by February 1, 2000 if they
plan to attend the Joint Meetings.  Those abstracts must be submitted
following the ASA abstract submission instructions described in AMSTAT
News.  Students selected for inclusion in the session will receive
further information about abstract submission and fee waivers from the
award committee.

Information on the competition can also be accessed on the website of
the Statistical Computing section.  A current pointer to the website
is available from the ASA website at www.amstat.org. Inquiries and
application materials should be emailed or mailed to:

messages.subject: RE: [S] creating a log or diary file in S-PLUS
messages.subject_clean: [S] creating a log or diary file in S-PLUS
messages.body_plain:
With the Unix version of S-PLUS, there are several ways to get a transcript
(i.e. a file of all the input to and output from S-PLUS).  Some suggestions,
in order of desirability:

1. Run S-PLUS within emacs, and save the buffer S-PLUS is running in.  ESS
(http://www.stat.math.ethz.ch/ESS/) has lots of useful features for running
S-PLUS in emacs, and for editing transcripts.

2. Use the "script" command.  This isn't available on all versions of Unix,
but if you have it, just run it before you start S-PLUS, and press control-D
from the shell to close the script after quitting S-PLUS.

        % script
        Script started, file is typescript
        % Splus
        ...
        > q()
        % <control-D>
        Script done, file is typescript

The transcript can be found in the file "typescript".

3. Run S-PLUS in an x-term and either use a long scrollback buffer (xterm
-sb -sl 10000) and cut-and-paste, or turn on logging (from the
ctrl-leftmouse menu).

4. Inside S-PLUS, use 
        options(echo=T)
        sink("transcript")
   This last one is the least satisfactory, as you don't get to see the
S-PLUS output on the screen, and the transcript contains input and output
but no prompts to distinguish them.

On S-PLUS for Windows it's much easier -- just cut and paste from the
Commands window.  In order for this to be a comprehensive script, you should
also redirect output from script files to the commands window, with Options
| Text Output Routing.

Kind regards,
# David

--
David M Smith  (dsmith at mathsoft.co.uk)

messages.subject: RE: [S] Storage space hint
messages.body_plain:
This is a useful hint, but I'd add a couple of comments:

* Storing objects as single precision will reduce the amount of disk space
the object requires, but it won't necessarily reduce your memory
requirements if you pass the object to certain functions.  This is because
functions such as lm() which pass data to a C or Fortran routine will
probably have to convert it to double precision first.  (Most of the
underlying C and Fortran code in S-PLUS is now double-precision.)

* convert.col.type was undocumented in S-PLUS 4.5, but *is* documented in
S-PLUS 2000.  It's not available on the Unix versions of S-PLUS.

# David

> From: owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> [mailto:owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu]On Behalf Of Michael Camilleri
> Sent: 29 September 1999 22:21
> To: 's-news at wubios.wustl.edu'
> Subject: [S] Storage space hint
> 
> 
> 
> For those that don't know already, you can half the storage 
> space for a
> numeric object by specifying single precision.  There are at 
> least 3 ways to
> do this:
> 
> 1) For a vector:
> storage.mode(x) <- "single"
> 
> 2) For a matrix or data frame
> data <- convert.col.type(target = data, column.spec = 1:ncol(data), 
>               column.type = "single")
> This function appears to be undocumented
> 
> or for(i in 1:ncol(data)) storage.mode(data[,i]) <- "single"
> 
> 3)Use the Data|Change Data Type menu (which calls (2))
> 
> Well worth doing if you have large data sets and don't need 
> double precision
> accuracy. It does not appear to affect any Splus analyses.
> 
> use the object.size(x) function to find out how many bytes 
> your object uses.
> 
> Cheers!
> Michael Camilleri

messages.subject: [S] xyplot
messages.body_plain:
I would like to thank those who offered their answers to my question
regarding xyplot. Why STATSCI asks us to pay license maintanence fee
every year and it does not offer the same kind of service that
this news group provide? 

Nick Ellis, John Thaden, Jose Pinheiro, Renard Lancelot, Robert Key
and Max Kuhn offered their help to my question. Thank you so much!
A great resource for learning xyplot or Trellis plot in general is

http://cm.bell-labs.com/cm/ms/departments/sia/project/trellis

I did not check but Jose Pinheiro indicated that there is a buildin
function in nlme 3.1 that augments predicted values. It is called
augPred().

Original problem was:
 mydata.nlme <- nlme( .......,data=mydata,......)
 xyplot( resp ~ expl | facA*facB,
         data= mydata,
         ylab='Response',
         xlab='Explanatory',
         panel=function(x,y) {
          panel.xyplot(x,y)
          yhat<- fitted(mydata.nlme)
          panel.xyplot(x,yhat$population,type='l')
          }
        )

solution:
 mydata.nlme <- nlme( .......,data=mydata,......)
 yhat <- fitted(mydata.nlme)
 xyplot( resp ~ expl | facA*facB,
         data=mydata,
         ylab='Response',
         xlab='Explanatory',
         panel=function(x,y,subscripts) {
          panel.xyplot(x,y)
          panel.xyplot(x,yhat$population[subscripts],type='p',pch='+')
         }
       )

Remarks:
*I did not use type='l' because the lines are wrapped around. It has
 to do with sorting my facA*facB some how.
*The panel labels are different if I change facA & facB to numeric.

I will iron out some of these minor details. Thank you for all your
help.

Winson Taam
Department of Math. & Stat.
Oakland University
Rochester, MI 48309

messages.subject: Re: [S] Repeating a Data Frame
messages.body_plain:
Hi Allen,

How's tricks?

> I've got a dataframe I'll call "Dat" that I'd like to repeat 27 times.
> I want to do something like
>   BigDat <- rbind(rep(Dat, 27))
> but that doesn't work like I want when Dat is a dataframe.  
> It just creates the same number of rows with my columns repeated 27 times.
> I want BigDat to have the same number of columns with 27 times as many rows.
> 
> Can someone show me how to do this?

I think it needs a loop.  The simplest is certainly

BigDat <- NULL
for(i in 1:27) BigDat <- rbind(BigDat, Dat)

If 27 really is the number and you want to do this sort of thing
all the time you can slick things up just slightly by

BigDat <- Dat
for(i in 1:3) BigDat <- rbind(BigDat, BigDat, BigDat)

[think about it...]

You can hide the loop in various clever ways, such as

BigDat <- do.call("rbind", lapply(1:27, function(x) Dat))

but I'd be very surprised if you gained all that much...

Bill.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Repeating a Data Frame
messages.body_plain:
> 
> How about a variant of this problem, where we want
>  to repeat the i th row of Dat nreps[i] times?

Charles Berry pointed out the obvious efficient solution that
solves this as well as the previous problem - use an index
vector!  The idea can be made into a one-line function:

rep.matrix <- 
    function(matrix, ...) matrix[rep(seq(1:nrow(matrix)), ...), ]

The `matrix' argument can be a genuine matrix or any matrix-like
structure such as a data frame.  The ... argument can be a times=
or a length.out= argument, as for rep().

So the original problem would be solved using

BigDat <- rep.matrix(Dat, times = 27)

or

BigDat <- rep.matrix(Dat, length.out = 27*nrow(Dat)) 

(if you want to be a little obscure) and the new problem would be
handled by

BigDat <- rep.matrix(Dat, times = nreps)

[Hmm.  Now why didn't I think of that?  :-)]

This same idea is handy if ever you need to bootstrap a data
frame, of course:

Dat.boot <- Dat[sample(1:nrow(Dat), nrow(Dat), rep = T), ]

but if you were bootstrapping a fitted model it would be better
to use sample() to generate a subset vector and update on it
rather than make a duplicate copy of the data frame.

Bill Venables.

to the list.  I'd appreciate precise references to the source

messages.subject: [S] SPlus-Oracle - summary
messages.body_plain:
A few weeks ago, I asked about SPLUS-Oracle interaction.
I received several responses. 
It turns out that the possibilities include installing the ODBC driver 
when one is working with Splus for windows (Nick Ellis (also see Rose 
O'Connor), Howard Brill, Jens Oehlschlaegel-Akiyoshi, Cheryl Howard), 
going via SAS (Anona Thorne), HTML based work (Amara Graps) and direct 
import of Oracle data by SPlus 5.1 for UNIX (Mette Langaas). 

Huge thanks to all of you for sending me so much detailed information 
in such a short time.

Best regards

Sucharita Ghosh
rita.ghosh at wsl.ch

The messages are forwarded below.

-------------
From: "Ellis, Nick (Marine, Cleveland)" <Nick.Ellis at cmis.csiro.au>

At our site we have an Oracle database on a Solaris machine. I have an
ODBC driver installed on my Windows NT machine. I can query the database
through the ODBC driver. The ODBC driver can be used from various
applications like MS Access and Splus. From Splus (4.5 for Windows) you
click on File | Import Data... | From ODBC connection. Ask an administrator
to set up the ODBC driver for you.

Nick Ellis
CSIRO Marine Research   mailto:Nick.Ellis at marine.csiro.au
PO Box 120                      ph    +61 (07) 3826 7260
Cleveland QLD 4163      fax   +61 (07) 3826 7222
Australia                       http://www.marine.csiro.au
-------------
From: Rosemary O'Connor [mailto:rosemary.oconnor at marine.csiro.au] 
(confirming the response of Nick Ellis)

The only problem is that with SPlus it is not dynamic. ie a copy of the
data is imported, changes are not reflected in the database. Also if 
the database tables change a new copy needs to be imported.

Rosemary O'Connor                  
Data Manager             
Cleveland Laboratories         
CSIRO Division of Marine Research  
 
Phone:  (07) 3826 7298
Fax  :  (07) 3826 7222
Email:  Rosemary.O'Connor at marine.csiro.au

--------------
From: Howard Brill <HBrill at MonroePlan.com>

I've done this using SYBASE SQL ANYWHERE via the ODBC driver in S-PLUS
4.5 on a PC. The same technique should work with Oracle. You can submit
a SQL statement through S-PLUS's ODBC import dialog.

-------------
From: "Cheryl Howard" <cherylghoward at hotmail.com>

The best way to get Oracle data into S-Plus is to use the ODBC interface.  
In S-Plus under the file menu, select Import Data> From ODBC Connection... In 
the dialog  box you can use a SQL query to pull only a portion of the 
database into S-Plus.  In order to do this, you need to have the Oracle 
ODBC driver installed.  The drivers can be found on your Oracle CD.

Cheryl G. Howard, D.Sc.
cherylghoward at hotmail.com
----------------------------

From: anona at hivnet.ubc.ca

The only way I've done this is to go from oracle to Sas, where I do some
preliminary work, and then from Sas to Splus.  If you need further details,
let me know.  Perhaps by now, someone has given you information about 
a more direct route.

Anona Thorne
Canadian HIV Trials Network
Vancouver, B.C.
-------------
From: Amara Graps <Amara.Graps at mpi-hd.mpg.de>
(Already published on the SNEWS)

-------------
From: "Dr. Jens Oehlschlaegel-Akiyoshi" <oehl at geocities.com>

the S+for windows (from version 4.0) allows ODBC-Access, which in turn 
would allow accessing Oracle.

Dr. Jens Oehlschlaegel-Akiyoshi
Psychologist/Statistician (Ph.D.)
Microsoft Certified Systems Engineer (MCSE)

oehl at geocities.com    http://www.geocities.com/Tokyo/Bay/5663/
-------------
From: Mette Langaas <Mette.Langaas at nr.no>

I have checked this out for Splus=SPlus 5.1 for UNIX. It seems that data
can be imported into S-Plus from oracle (I managed to do that) but
S-Plus kan not export data to oracle. Therefore I ended up by using
ascii files for import and export Splus-oracle.

If you are interested in details on how to import data from oracle into
S-Plus 5.1 UNIX I can send you an example -- but let me know if you are
interested as soon as possible (I'm starting on my maternal leave Oct
7).

Mette Langaas
Mette.Langaas at nr.no
http://www.nr.no/~mette

(I will inform the list, if I hear from Mette again. But possibly, she is 
already on leave and all the best to her.... ).

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary of "Reapeating a Data Frame (rows of) 27 Times"
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who replied.  My original question was how to repeat the rows
of data frame "Dat" 27 times, with the suggestion that something like
rbind(rep(Dat, 27)) ought to work.

The most efficient and intuitively pleasing (to me) answer came from Sam
Buttrey, Bill Dunlap, Tim Hesterberg, and Joseph Verducci who suggested the
result below.  As an reply to some recent s-news responses attributing the
first solution to Tim, I'll mention that Sam was actually the first to send
me a personal reply with this nice and very simple and efficient solution.
  > BigDat <- Dat[rep (1:nrow(Dat), 27),] 
Charles Berry also sent basically the same idea, which Bill Venables
expanded upon.

As always, I learned useful concepts from several of the answers, so I
summarize them below along with the time required to implement them on my PC
for one of my data sets.  Thanks again to all.

Allen Humbolt
Koch Industries, Inc.
humbolta at kochind.com

SOLUTIONS
1. Bill Venables, Nick Locantore, Tim Hesterberg      67.70 sec.
> BigDat <- NULL                     
> for(i in 1:27) BigDat <- rbind(BigDat, Dat) 
2. Bill Venables                                      15.93 sec.
> BigDat <- do.call("rbind", lapply(1:27, function(x) Dat)) 
3. Sam Buttrey, Bill Dunlap, Joseph Verducci           0.45 sec.
> BigDat <- Dat[rep (1:nrow(Dat), 27),] 
4. Peter Perkins                                      didn't work
> BigDat <- Dat
> BigDat <- data.frame(1:(27*nrow(Dat)),Dat)[,-1]
However, Peter's solution was efficient and took 1.03 minutes for me via
Splus 2000.
I didn't check the details of what I did carefully; but the interesting
question may be why this did not work on Splus 4.5, but did on 2000.  My
project
was on Splus 4.5 so I didn't bother to try all these examples on it.  I
tried it
on 2000 only because I was curious why I couldn't get it to work.
5. Erin Hodgess            Wouldn't finish; but did finish for smaller
problem.
> BigDat <- data.frame(t(rep(data.frame(t(Dat)),5))) 
6. Chuck Taylor                                       11.47 sec.
> doit <- paste("rbind(", paste(rep("Dat", 27), collapse=","), ")") 
>  eval(parse(text=doit)) 
7. Charles Berry                                       0.44 sec
> BigDat <- data.frame(Dat)[rep(1:318, 27)]  # Dat is 318 x 27
8. Bill Venables, who attributed to Charles Berrry     0.46 sec
> rep.matrix <-                                       
+  function(matrix, ...) matrix[rep(seq(1:nrow(matrix)), ...), ] 
> BigDat <- rep.matrix(Dat, times = 27)

messages.subject_clean: [S] Addendum to Summary of"Repeating a Data Frame (rows of) 27 Times "
messages.body_plain:
Tim Hesterberg followed up to help me understand an even more efficient
solution that he had previously presented to me.
Given my desire to repeat dataframe "Dat" 27 times:
  > attr(Dat, "dup.row.names") <- T
  > BigDat <- Dat[rep(1:nrow(Dat), 27) , ]
The addition of the attr statement reduced the time required on Splus 2000
from 0.47 seconds to 0.23 seconds.  As pointed out by Tim, there's no
efficiency improvement using Splus Version 4.5.  I'll add that you'll see
the same thing on Unix Version 3.4 compared to Unix Version 5.0 of Splus.
There's no efficiency improvement via 3.4; but there is significant
improvement via 5.0.

Also, in my SOLUTIONS section I incorrectly identified Tim with the first
solution I presented.  He presented the solution above (along with three
others) and added the hint above about using attr.

I also found an irrelevant line my copying of Peter Perkins' solution.  I
should have simply stated:
  > BigDat <- data.frame(1:(27*nrow(Dat)), Dat)[, -1]
instead of including the extraneous line before it.  Since I had mentioned
that this solution succeeds in Splus 2000 while it fails in Splus 4.5, I
wanted to correct this detail for anyone interested in pursuing why Splus
2000 performs differently than Splus 4.5 using Peter's syntax.

Finally, in an e-mail I just received, Jeff Longmate points out that 
  > Dat[rep(1:ncol(Dat), times=27) , ]
differs from
  > Dat[rep(1:ncol(Dat), each=27) , ]
in terms of the sort of the data. 

Allen Humbolt

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Not enough labels on x-axis
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Not enough labels on x-axis
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

I got several responses to my question regarding tick mark's labels (see
the following original posting).  Some suggested to put the tick marks and
their associated labels in two or more steps, others suggested to reduce
the font size through the cex parameter.  The suggestion I prefer so far is
from Bill Dunlap who suggested to draw the tick marks and their labels one
at time in a loop, he suggested a little function to do that; you will find
his solution after the original posting.

Thanks again to all who responded,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat
télephone            : (418) 835-8839
télecopieur          : (418) 835-5865
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at spgdag.ca

"In God we trust all others must bring data"

Original posting:

> in the following bit of code I woul like S+ to produce a label for each
> tick mark of the x-axis, typically between 2 and 12 for my application,
but
> when there is more than 5 or 6 tick marks S+ doesn't give me a label for
all
> of them, why and how to force it to do it?  Note that "mylabels" has a
> label for each tick mark specified by "at = ".
>
>       plot(c(1:nrow(mat.plot)), mat.plot[,1], type = 'b', col = 1,
>               main = paste(names(factors)[i], '-', sinistre, sep = ' '),
>               xlab = '',
>               ylab = 'Differentiel',
>               axes = F,
>               ylim = c(-max(mat.plot[,1]), max(mat.plot[,1])))
>       axis (side = 1, at = c(1:nrow(mat.plot)), labels =
>             abbreviate(mylabels, minlength = 6),
>             crt = 45)

Bill Dunlap's solution:

axis() thinks it is doing you a favor by not printing labels it thinks
would overlap, but it doesn't have a good idea of how big the labels
really are and may not pay attention to the rotation you specified.
You can call axis() in a loop, printing one tick mark with each
iteration.  E.g., define my.axis which loops over at and labels

     my.axis <- function(side, at, labels, ...)
          for(i in seq(along=at))
               axis(side=side, at=at[i], labels=labels[i], ...)

and call it just like you call axis:

     my.axis (side = 1, at = c(1:nrow(mat.plot)),
          labels =abbreviate(mylabels, minlength = 6), crt = 45)

I want to group my time until event field (days)  into monthly time
intervals (i.e.
[0-30), [30-60),.....).  Is there an argument with any of the "survival"
functions that will allow me to do this, either by stipulating the
upper/lower bounds or the number of intervals I desire.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Are round() and digits= broken?
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Are round() and digits= broken?
messages.body_plain:
My inquiry was about making nicely formatted output with round() or 
print(object,digits=).  Several correspondents (Brian Ripley, Todd Taylor, 
and Sam Buttrey) pointed out that those functions don't work as I thought 
they did and that for nicely formatted output, format() is needed.

I had not realized that despite options, S-Plus drops trailing zeros from 
numbers with decimal points (when printing).  That was the specific cause 
of my confusion.

Some fiddling with format() and paste() has resulted in output that is neat 
and easy to read.  My thanks to all who responded -- including those who 
(because of Net lags) will respond after I post this summary.

--

messages.subject: [S] Circular Histograms: Summary
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to all who wrote in response to my query about circular
histograms.   The most useful programs (for my purposes) came from Mario
Borja, Megan Pledger and Colin Farrow.   Mario Borja pointed me to the book
by Nick Fisher "Statistical Analysis of Circular Data", Cambridge University
Press, 1995, and attached some very useful code written by Nick Fisher that
produces exactly what I need.  However, it ran out of space on the page when
I tried it with as few as 1000 observations, and I have 7000.  I'm sure I
can make some adjustments that will allow it to work, though.  If anyone is
interested in this code, please respond directly to me and I will forward
it.  It is too large to attach here for all the group, though.

Megan Pledger and Colin Farrow each provided me with much simpler code that
also produced nice circular histograms and perhaps will be more appropriate
for my 7000 observations.  Their codes follow.

Once again, the S+ community has been most kind and generous in sharing
their knowledge and I sure appreciate it.

Manuela Huso
Statistician
Department of Forest Science
321D Richardson Hall
Oregon State University
Corvallis, OR   97331-5752
541.737.6232
Manuela.Huso at orst.edu

Nick Fisher's graphic:
 <<...>> 

Megan Pledger's Code:

The code is below.

# It takes 4 parameters
# heights    - the heights to make the bars
# sig        - the number of significant digits to write the numbers on the
contour lines
# angle      - the angle of the first bar, the default is 0 which equal East
# main.title - the title for the plot 

# It requires a vector of frequencies
#   the length of the vector determines the number of spokes
# An example call is
# circular.histogram(rpois(72,12),4,main.title="Directions of the Mexican
Dung Beetle")

 <<...>> 

# The heights of the bars are measured from the inner white circle. 

circular.histogram<-
function(heights,  sig, angle = 0,main.title="")
{
        par.to.keep<-par()      
        par(pty = "s", mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0), mgp = c(0, 0, 0), new = F)
        plot(0, 0, axes = F, xlim = c(-8, 8), ylim = c(-8, 8), xlab = "",
ylab =
"", type = "n")
        par(xaxs = "d", yaxs = "d", new = T)
        heights.length <- length(heights)
        full.angle <- (2 * pi)/heights.length
        half.angle <- full.angle/2
        x <- matrix(0, heights.length + 1, 1)
        y <- x
        y[1] <- sin(angle - half.angle)
        x[1] <- cos(angle - half.angle)
        scaled.heights <- heights/max(heights) * 7
        for(k in 1:heights.length) {
                x[k + 1] <- cos(angle - half.angle + k * full.angle)
                y[k + 1] <- sin(angle - half.angle + k * full.angle)
                xlower <- cos(angle + (k - 1) * full.angle) *
scaled.heights[k] + x[k]
                xupper <- cos(angle + (k - 1) * full.angle) *
scaled.heights[k] + x[k + 1]
                ylower <- sin(angle + (k - 1) * full.angle) *
scaled.heights[k] + y[k]
                yupper <- sin(angle + (k - 1) * full.angle) *
scaled.heights[k] + y[k + 1]
                polygon(c(x[k], xlower, xupper, x[k + 1]), c(y[k], ylower,
yupper, y[k +
1]))
        }
        polygon(x, y, density = -1)
        symbols(0, 0, circles = 1, axes = F, add = T, inch = F, col = 0)
        symbols(c(0,0), c(0,0), circles = c(8,4.5), axes = F, add = T, inch
= F, col = 1,lty=2)
                par(adj=0.5,cex=2)
                mtext(main.title,3,line=-1,outer=T)
        par(adj=0,cex=1.5)
        text( sin(heights.length/8 * full.angle)*8,   cos( heights.length/8
* full.angle)*8, paste(signif(max(heights),sig)))
        text( sin(heights.length/8 * full.angle)*4.5, cos(heights.length/8
* full.angle)*4.5, paste(signif(max(heights)/2,sig)))
        par(cex=1.5,adj=0.5)
        text(0,8,"N")
                text(0,-8,"S")
                par(adj=0.5)
                text(-8,0,"E")
                text(8,0,"W") 
        box()
        par(xaxs = "r", yaxs = "r")
        par(par.to.keep)
        invisible()
}

Collin Farrow's Code:

# az - a vector of directions
# circ - controls the spacing of cicular gridlines
# start - the start angle for the first rose, default 0
# step - the class interval for each petal, default 30 degrees
# legend - logical - is a legend required
# grid - logical - is a grid required

# so something like
# data are a vector of dispersal directions in whole degrees, one for each
owl

owls<-round(runif(1000,0,360))
ear(owls, step=5, circ=c(0.25,0.5,0.75,1)) 

# should get you started
 <<...>> 

ear <- function(az, circ = 1:4, start = 0, step = 30, legend = T, grid = F,
...)
{
        oldpar <- par(usr = c(-1, 1, -1, 1), pty = "s")
        if(is.matrix(az)) {
                naz1 <- nrow(az)
                az <- az[, 1]
        }
        else {
                naz1 <- length(az)
                az <- c(az, az + 180)
                if(max(az) > 359)
                        az[az > 359] <- az[az > 359] - 360
        }
        n <- round(360/step)
        class <- (0:n) * step
        h <- hist(az, plot = F, breaks = class)
        h$breaks <- h$breaks + start
        naz <- length(az)
        rci <- (step * pi)/180
        r <- sqrt((2 * 1 * h$count)/(naz1 * rci))
        ncirc <- length(circ)
        pc <- circ/10
        f <- pc * naz
        cr <- sqrt((2 * 1 * f)/(naz * rci))
        zero <- rep(0, ncirc)
        sr <- (.95 * r)/max(r, cr)
        scr <- (.95 * cr)/max(r, cr)
        for(i in 1:n) {
                if(sr[i] > 0) {
                        a1 <- h$breaks[i]
                        a2 <- h$breaks[i + 1]
                        a <- ((a1:a2) * pi)/180
                        x <- cos(a) * sr[i]
                        y <- sin(a) * sr[i]
                        xx <- c(0, y, 0)
                        yy <- c(0, x, 0)
                        polygon(xx, yy, ...)
                }
        }
        grid <- ifelse(circ[1] > 0, T, F)
       if(grid) {
                symbols(zero, zero, circles = scr, add = T, inch = F)
                points(0, scr[ncirc], pch = 3)
        }
        if(legend) {
                mtext(paste("N=", naz1, "Max radius=", max(h$counts)), 1, 1)
                if(grid) {
                        tmp <- paste(circ * 10, "%", sep = "", collapse = "
")
                        mtext(paste("circles at", tmp), 1, 3)
                }
        }
        par(oldpar)
        invisible(NULL)
}

messages.subject: [S] Proportional odds (summary)
messages.body_plain:
My question was:
> Can anyone advise me how to fit the proportional odds model for ordinal
> multinomial responses (as in section 9.4 of Agresti, Categorical Data
> Analysis), using Splus (or R)?
>
As usual, replies were prompt and informative. There are two functions
in widely used libraries, and it seems best to just quote the respective
authors:
***************
>>From Brian Ripley:
Without that book to hand, I think this is the procedure in

polr in the current MASS library (and examples in V&R3)
lrm in Harrell's library Design.

Neither currently work in R.
*************
>>From Bill Venables:
In the latest version of the MASS library there is a function,
polr (for "proportional odds log-linear regression"...) that I
suspect will do the trick.  It follows McCullagh's paper.  The
thing is also illustrated in the latest V&R (3rd Edition)
*************
>>From Frank Harrell:
In the Design S-Plus library (from statlib or the web address below, and
note that Design also
requires the Hmisc library - from the same place) the lrm function will do
what you want.  -Frank

http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat
************

In addition, under the category of "why not talk to your colleagues
first", there is software under development by Thomas Yee
<yee at scitec.Auckland.ac.nz>

My VGAM software will do it, plus more.  See
http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/yee/vgam 
I can give you a demonstration of it if you want.

Thomas
**************

Many thanks to these and all other respondents (John Maindonald, Alan
Zaslavsky, and possibly someone else whose email I have already deleted
because it reiterated previous suggestions)

messages.subject: [S] answer to 2-scale graphics question
messages.body_plain:
My question was:
> I try to do a simple graphic that plots 2 series on 2 different scales,
the
> first series should refer to a scale plotted on a left y-axis and the
other
> on a right y-axis. I find nothing on that topic in the splus book or in
the
> faq. Someone can help?

First, thank you to everybody who took the time to get to me on this
question. 
Of course, all the answers are a little bit different but the "consensual
answer" is: 
(I reproduce here the message of Z.Todd Taylor)

**************************************************************************

The general approach is to just make two plots, one on top of
the other.  You have to lie to Splus about what you're doing
and take manual control of axes...

   # First series...
   tsplot(data1)

   # Lie to Splus, telling it it has a clean slate to draw on
   # so it needn't go to a new page...
   par(new=T)

   # Second series, careful not to clobber existing axis...
   tsplot(data2, axes=F)

   # Manually add on second axis...
   axis(side=4)

You'll also need to worry about axis labels and such, but you
get the idea.

*************************************************************************

Again, thank you very much to:

Bill Dunlap, Z.Todd Taylor, Stephen Smith, Erin Hodgess, Peter Perkins, Anne
York, Berwin Turlach, Naomi Robbins, Nick Ellis, Marcel Baumgartner,
Christian Keller, Wolfgang Hannoever and Renaud Lancelot from United States,
Germany, Australia, Switzerland and Senegal. Thank you to all the world  :o)

Patrick

messages.subject: [S] Grouping treatment means by least significant difference.
messages.subject_clean: [S] Grouping treatment means by least significant difference.
messages.body_plain:
Several weeks ago I asked a question about ideas along this line.  Nobody
seemed to have what I was looking for, so this is something I came up with.

Below are two functions, "LSD" and "duncan.groups" that group treatment
means according to the method described in Steel&Torrie with output format
inspired by the way SAS displays the same results.  It's not very elegant,
but I managed to use only one "for" loop.  It would be nice to have a
graphical display of the same information....any takers?

Given a dataset D with a model Y~Trt, here's how I would use the functions:

>treat.means_as.matrix(rev(sort(tapply(D$Y,D$Trt,mean))))
>D.aov_aov(Y~Trt,data=D,qr=T)
>anova(D.aov)
>print(duncan.groups(treat.means[,1],LSD(D.aov)),quote=F)
>LSD(D.aov)

and here is the results which are produced.  The output shows the means in
groups (A,B,...) such that within each group, the difference in the means is
less than the LSD.  It works for me, but your mileage may vary.

             Mean Gr Gr Gr Gr 
  CONTROL 165.006 A          
     PROP 120.868    B       
H15 G 5E4 64.063        C    
H15 S 1E5 22.557           D 
H15 S 5E4 20.505           D 
H15 S 4E5 16.809           D 
H15 G 1E5 13.153           D 
H15 G 1E6 5.781            D 
H15 S 1E6 2.971            D 
H15 G 4E5 0.666            D 
--> LSD(D.aov)
[1] 38.35334

"LSD"<-
function(data.aov)
{
        dfResid <- data.aov$df.residual
        stderr <- model.tables(data.aov,type="means",se = T)$se$Trt[1]
        lsd <- qt(0.975, dfResid) * stderr
        lsd
}

"duncan.groups"<-
function(meanvec, lsd)
{
# Inputs
# meanvec : vector of means, sorted largest to smallest
# lsd : least significant difference
# Output
# Matrix with letters in columns that indicate groupings of means which
# are not significantly different.  Aka Duncan's method.  Output
# is similar to that provided by SAS, though not quite as compact.
# Note : Only supports 26 groupings
        if(meanvec[1] - rev(meanvec)[1] < lsd) {
                group <- rep("A", length(meanvec))
                groupmatrix <- cbind(meanvec, group)
        }
        else {
                diffmat <- abs(outer(meanvec, meanvec, "-"))    
        # Difference matrix.  Entries with
                diffmat[diffmat > lsd] <- "Yes" 
        # "Yes" are significantly different.
                diffmat[diffmat != "Yes"] <- "N"
                diffmat[lower.tri(diffmat)] <- ""
                group.char <- 1
                curr.row <- diffmat[1,  ]
                curr.row.Yes <- pmatch("Yes", curr.row) 
        # Column where the first "Yes" occurs.
                group <- curr.row
                group[group == "N"] <- LETTERS[group.char]
                group.char <- group.char + 1
                groupmatrix <- group
                for(i in 2:nrow(diffmat)) {
                        prev.row <- curr.row
                        curr.row <- diffmat[i,  ]
                        prev.row.Yes <- curr.row.Yes
                        curr.row.Yes <- pmatch("Yes", curr.row)
                        if(is.na(curr.row.Yes))
                                curr.row.Yes <- -1
                        if(curr.row.Yes != prev.row.Yes) {
# Create a new group if needed
                                group <- curr.row
                                group[group == "N"] <- LETTERS[group.char]
                                groupmatrix <- cbind(groupmatrix, group)
                                group.char <- group.char + 1
                        }
                        groupmatrix[groupmatrix == "Yes"] <- ""
                }
                groupmatrix <- cbind(meanvec, groupmatrix)
        }
        colnames <- c("Mean", rep("Gr", ncol(groupmatrix) - 1))
        rownames <- dimnames(groupmatrix)[[1]]
        dimnames(groupmatrix) <- list(rownames, colnames)
        groupmatrix
}

Kevin Wright, Pioneer Hi-Bred Int'l

messages.body_plain:
My original posting was:

> Within a for() loop, I fit a list of models (lme() function), some of
> them failing to converge or producing errors (singularities, etc.),
> resulting in an aborted loop.
> 
> How can I ignore these errors, so that the for() loop goes to the end ?

Many thanks to Bill Dunlap, Brian Ripley, Douglas Bates, Henrik Aalborg
Nielsen and Bert Gunter for their helpful replies. Three kinds of
solution were suggested:
1. try()
2. restart()
3. options(args)

The third solution was not appropriate in my case (sorry, I should have
given an example), and I was scared by the restart() help file:

...
DETAILS

This is a function to be used only by the adept and strong at heart. Use
of restart can be dangerous to your health and social standing. In
particular, if the function calling restart has an error, an infinite
loop of errors can easily result; such a loop can be terminated only
with Ctrl-Alt-Del or a system reset.  
...

So I turned to Bill Dunlap's solution (solution 1 below), which
perfectly met my needs. Since I use S+ 4.5, I had to implement the try()
function.

Here is a successful example of what I wanted to do:

### form is a character vector containing formulae
### e.g.
###> form[1]
###[1] "Weight ~ Age+Age2+Sex"

> mod <- lme(fixed = Weight ~ Age + Age2, random = ~ Age + Age2 | Id, data=wt1)
> for(i in 1:length(form)) assign(paste("mod.", i, sep=""), try(update(mod, 
> fixed = formula(form[i]))), where=1, immediate=T)

Many thanks again to everybody,

Best regards,

Renaud

########### Solution 1
Use the try() function, which was added to Splus 2000.
        try(expression)
will never stop the expression it is in.  It returns the value of
expression if there were no errors, otherwise it returns an object
of class "Error" containing the error message.  You will see the
error messages printed but the loop will continue.  E.g.,

> a <- list(try(lm(Murder~., data=data.frame(state.x77), subset=Area>5e5)),
+           try(lm(Murder~., data=data.frame(state.x77),
subset=Area>1e5)))
Error in lm.fit.qr(x, y): computed fit is singular, rank 1
 
Dumped
> a
[[1]]:
[1] "Error in lm.fit.qr(x, y): computed fit is singular, rank 1\n"
attr([[1]], "class"):
[1] "Error"
 
[[2]]:
Call:
lm(formula = Murder ~ ., data = data.frame(state.x77), subset = Area >
100000)
 
Coefficients:
 (Intercept)   Population      Income Illiteracy  Life.Exp    HS.Grad 
    97.33729 0.0003481624 0.005840989   5.118651 -1.480468 -0.3406841
      Frost          Area 
 0.04276222 -2.099673e-05
 
Degrees of freedom: 8 total; 0 residual

If you don't have Splus 2000 then the following code for try() ought to
work:

try <- function(expr, first = T)
{
# evaluates expr (in frame of caller) and returns either
# its value or the error message (with class "Error").
# DO NOT USE THE 'first' ARGUMENT.
        restart(first)
        if(first) {
                first <- F
                expr
        }
        else {
                error.msg <- get.message()
                class(error.msg) <- "Error"
                error.msg
        }
}

########### Solution 2
# 2.1
Use restart, carefully. See nlsList for an example.

# 2.2
You should check the documentation for the restart() function to see
how to do this.  Examples of the use of restart are in the functions
lmList and nlsList in the NLME library.

There was also a recent enquiry on S-news or nlme-help about this so
you can look for that answer (sorry but I don't have the reference for
that posting available).

# 2.3 (S-News Archives)
> > 3. As an absolute last resort, and with great care and attention, cautiously
> > approach the restart() function.  It is designed to step over failing
> > calculations in exactly this sort of context, but it is not for the faint
> > hearted.  You can do a lot of damage with this one...
> 
> I agree with everything that Bill says, especially trying the
> "plinear" algorithm.  Before trying to use the restart function
> yourself, you might check the nlsList function from the NLME library
> and see if you can use that.  It implements the approach that Bill
> describes.

There is a function in S Poetry called "ignore.error" which is a
general solution to escaping an error condition in cases where
there isn't an easy workaround. It uses "restart" as Bill
suggested.

# 2.4 NLME - Help Archives
> whenever the calling nlme function issues an error message (fails to
> converge or the matrix is not invertible, ...), my function is terminated
> immediately. Is there a way to write a function so that it
> continues to run
> after a nlme error message.

Here is a function that I have used for nlme simulations.  I think I
found
it among the "splus tips" page of the splus website.  Call nlme( ) as
the
expr argument to the following function:

function(expr, first = T)
{
        if(!missing(first))
                stop("Do not supply the argument 'first'")
        restart(T)
        if(first) {
                first <- F
                expr
        }
        else {
                structure(class = "error", list(message =
.C("get_last_message",
                        "")[[1]], expression = substitute(expr)))
        }
}

The function will store the error messages until your function is
complete
and then spit them out at the end.

########### Solution 3
# 3.1
>>From the help-page on options I have:

error=:   function (with no arguments) to be called when an error
       or  interrupt  occurs.   S-PLUS  provides  dump.calls  and
       dump.frames to dump the outstanding function calls or  the
       entire associated frames.  See the documentation for these
       functions for details.  The option  error=NULL  eliminates
       all error actions.
interrupt=:    function (with no arguments) to be called when  an
       interrupt  occurs.   The  function  is called in the frame
       active when the interrupt happens and  can  be  used,  for
       example,  to  examine  current  objects, to change values,
       etc.  If two interrupts occur  in  a  row,  the  interrupt
       action  is  not  executed;  instead  the  error  action is
       carried  out.   The   option   interrupt=NULL   eliminates
       interrupt actions.

I think options(error=NULL) or options(interrupt=NULL) will do the job.

# 3.2
AT the beginning of your function:
err<-options(error=NULL)  #saves error state

At the end of your function:
options(err)  #restores original error state

--

ISRA-LNERV
BP 2057 Dakar-Hann
Senegal

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Overlaying plots
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users,

a few days ago I had a request concerning the specification of y-axes when
overlaying two plots on the same page, see original querry at the end of
this message.  I got a single response, from Melanie Cox (thanks Melanie).
The approach suggested by Melanie is:

subplot(expression ( {
 plot(...............)
 axis(...............)
#etc

}
), other arguments to subplot)

 Although it looked promising I haven't tried this approach.  I ended up
using

par(xaxs = 'd', new = T)

between the call to "barplot" and the call to "plot" (I had to switch the
order in which I was calling the two plotting
functions.) and resetting the xaxs parameter to 'r' after the second plot.
  Using this approach allowed me to specify
the right and left y-axes as I pleased and the "direct x-axis style"
allowed me to use the returned values of
barplot as my "x-values" for the call to plot, which is what I wanted;

Nice weekend to everyone,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat
télephone            : (418) 835-8839
télecopieur          : (418) 835-5865
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at spgdag.ca

"In God we trust all others must bring data"

a loop where several 2-plots pages are produced,

plots to be centered at the positions specified by the at argument of the
first call to axis and when I use axis(side = 4, ......) after the call to

messages.subject_clean: [S] Output of 'summary(aov(... + Error()))' for unbalanced designs
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users

As a non-expert in split-plot analysis of variance I need some
help in the interpretation of the output given by
      summary(aov(... + Error()))
for unbalanced designs. 

With the following data set (taken from the S-Plus manual)...

drug <- data.frame(y=c(75.9, 74.3, 80, 78.9, 78.3, 75.5,
                     79.6, 79.2, 80.3, 78.2, 80.4, 76.2,
                     80.7, 77.2, 82, 83.8,  80.3, 78.6,
                     81.4, 81.5, 80.1, 81.1, 81.9, 86.4),
                   gender=factor(rep(c("F","M"),c(12,12))),
                   time=ordered(rep(1:4,6)),
                   subject=factor(rep(1:6, rep(4,6))))

... I get the output (balanced design)

> summary(aov(y ~ gender*time + Error(subject), data=drug))
Error: subject 
          Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value   Pr(F) 
gender     1  60.80167 60.80167 19.32256 0.01173
Residuals  4  12.58667  3.14667                 

Error: Within 
            Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value     Pr(F) 
time         3  49.10833 16.36944 6.316184 0.0081378
gender:time  3  14.80167  4.93389 1.903751 0.1828514
Residuals   12  31.10000  2.59167

Now, omitting the first observation (--> unbalanced design) 
gives         

> summary(aov(y ~ gender*time + Error(subject), data=drug,
+             subset=-1))
Error: subject 
          Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value     Pr(F) 
gender     1  51.18368 51.18368 17.39709 0.0250881
time       1   1.16004  1.16004  0.39429 0.5745999
Residuals  3   8.82625  2.94208                   

Error: Within 
            Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value     Pr(F) 
time         3  48.13461 16.04487 6.598199 0.0081890
gender:time  3  17.60581  5.86860 2.413370 0.1219607
Residuals   11  26.74875  2.43170                   

Factor time appears twice in the table above.
Is this correct?
If it is, can anyone explain me how to interpret this?

Any help is greatly appreciated!

PS. Searching for a hint in old S-news I found the following
information...

> Date: Fri, 24 Apr 1998 10:12:23 +0930
> From: Bill Venables <wvenable at attunga.stats.adelaide.edu.au>
> Subject: Re: [S] Split-plot analysis
> ...
> ...
> Also it should be more widely understood that aov(... + Error())
> is very restricted in what it can do.  Unless your error
> structure is completely balanced (orthogonal and has equal cell
> sizes at all levels) the analysis will not be fully correct.  For
> example just one missing value renders the analysis technically
> incorrect, with *no warning or comment* from aov.  (With missing
> values you can repair most aspects of the analysis by the usual
> "dummy covariate" trick, but that's another long story.)

--

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to run a bootstrap (500 trials) of an iterative function in 
S-Plus 2000 with its service pack.  The datasets are relatively small, 
perhaps 1000 rows x 30 column all together.

I expected this to be slow going in an interpreted package, but it is much 
worse than I expected.

Computations started out quickly, but have bogged down incredibly.  This is 
on a dual-processor Pentium-III machine with 256Mb of RAM (and plenty of 
fast SCSI disk space).  At about halfway through the bootstrap, the Windows 
NT Task Manager indicates that S-Plus is generating hundreds of page faults 
a minute and is now using 194Kb of RAM.

What is wrong?  Is this a bug or some feature gone wild?  Is there some way 
to work around this?

Thanks!

--
Michael Prager                     <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516

> time         3  48.13461 16.04487 6.598199 0.0081890
> gender:time  3  17.60581  5.86860 2.413370 0.1219607
> Residuals   11  26.74875  2.43170                   
> 
> 
> Factor time appears twice in the table above.
> Is this correct?

This is awkward.  It is correct that time should appear twice, the Within
stratum analysis is correct, but the subject stratum analysis is partially
incorrect, although approximately correct.

> If it is, can anyone explain me how to interpret this?

The imbalance resulting from omitting the first observation has meant that
between subjects you have information about both sex (why do people say
`gender' when they mean `sex'?) and time, instead of only information on the
time factor when it was balanced.  The lack of balance, though, has meant that
the subject totals no longer have equal variances but no account has been taken
of this in forming the tests in that stratum (and it would be quite difficult
to do so by extending this paradigm).

Stratum by stratum analyses of variance are (in my view) best used for balanced
designs with orthogonal block structure and treatment structure such that each
component has information recoverable from one stratum only.  This pretty well
limits it to split plot experiments, but I guess BIBs where the interblock
treatment component is negligible would be OK, too.  For anything more
complicated nowdays I would use lme() where what used to be called "the
recovery of interblock information" sort of all comes out in the wash.

> 
> Any help is greatly appreciated!

I think the most useful thing I can say is that if you are going to be using
these tools frequently, don't dodge becoming "an expert".  It is a very
slippery and tricky area and not something you can leave to software and the
occasional query to S-news.  

I feel pretty strong about this: linear models could be one of the simplest and
most straightforward areas of statistical practice if only people were not so
terrified of linear algebra.  You can sort of get there without it but it
takes a lot longer, the result is never as good and prejudices easily take hold
along the way.  The real problem arises when the software starts to reinforce
the prejudices, but I digress...

> PS. Searching for a hint in old S-news I found the following
> information...
> 
> > Date: Fri, 24 Apr 1998 10:12:23 +0930

> > is very restricted in what it can do.  Unless your error
> > structure is completely balanced (orthogonal and has equal cell
> > sizes at all levels) the analysis will not be fully correct.  For
> > example just one missing value renders the analysis technically
> > incorrect, with *no warning or comment* from aov.  (With missing
> > values you can repair most aspects of the analysis by the usual
> > "dummy covariate" trick, but that's another long story.)

Tsk tsk.  Doesn't that sound pompous?  Did I say that?  Well it must be true,
then...  :-)  (The email address is no longer true, though.)   V.

The theories are not mutually exclusive.  What we have is another
example of an amazing ability to make mountains out of molehills.
"Gender" is one of the few words in the English language that has only
one meaning (even though it can be applied to plumbing fittings as
well as to people).  "Sex" is more normal in that it can have the
meaning of an attribute of an individual person AND it can also be use
to describe an activity involving people.

The post-modernist hokum has been here before with the word "man"
which until recently could be used to refer to an individual human
male adult (as distinct from an individual human female adult) AND it
could be used to refer to the human species as a whole -- young and
old, male and female, ancestors and decendants, etc., etc.  The
fixation on only one of the meanings of the word has brought about the
rise of such abominations as "spokespersonship".

Odd, really since nobody seems to have any problem with the fact that
"finger" is sometimes used to include "thumb" and at other times used
to distinguish from it; "day" sometimes includes hours of darkness and
other times excludes them.  The list is very, very long.

|> "gender" would be more appropriate than "sex", simply because

Given that there are influential people unwilling to deal with some of
the words of more than one meaning, and the idea doesn't seem to be
going out of fashion, there is a market for Sillyspeak for some time
yet.

Roll on post-post-modernism.

best

Patrick

messages.subject: [S] Sex/Gender
messages.body_plain:
A social scientist told me that 'gender' was coined
to signify the "sex" which a person identifies with, as opposed to
their actual biological sex (according to their DNA, say). 

So a male-to-female transsexual would have Sex=M and Gender=F. 
Also, rarely, abnormal foetal or childhood development leads to a person
appearing to be of one sex but being genetically of another sex.

Only social scientists are sophisticated enough to hold this
distinction clear in their minds. Everyone else has simply
substituted "Gender" for "Sex" throughout.
Leading to news-clippings like:

        "Bruce can determine the gender of a newly-hatched chicken
                 in 15 seconds"

        "Risk factors for decompression sickness include age, overweight, 
                and female gender. To reduce your risk of DCS it's important
                to maintain your fitness. Of course you can't do anything
                about your age or your gender"

Mostly I dislike the advent of "gender" because it ruined a 
good joke about statisticians!

----
Prof Adrian Baddeley, Mathematics & Statistics, University of Western Australia
                <http://maths.uwa.edu.au/~adrian/>

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Memory Leak or similar in S-Plus 2000?
messages.body_plain:
I thank those who replied with suggestions.  I am not in my office now and 
don't have their messages, so despite my gratitude, they will remain nameless.  
I also thank Tim Hesterberg of Mathsoft, who ran my code in an attempt to 
replicate the problem.  The response from Mathsoft was exceptionally prompt and 
thorough.

The problem I experienced was excessive and increasing memory use and 
drastically decreasing execution time of some S-Plus code of mine.  The code 
bootstraps a user-written function that itself is iterative.  The code is 
entirely in S-Plus and uses the bootstrap() function.

Tim's conclusion was this:  there is a bug in S-Plus 2000 that results in 
excessive memory buildup when such programs are run from a script file.  
However, if the commands are pasted into the command window and run that way, 
the memory buildup does not occur.  A bug report is being filed.

It was interesting to learn that a sequence of command can be pasted into the 
command window as a block and will be executed correctly.  I would not have 
expected that to work.

--

Beaufort, North Carolina

messages.subject: Re: [S] Sex vs. gender.
messages.body_plain:
This reminds me of something you see in the AIDS biz.  In AIDS, subjects
are often described by their "risk group", that is, the activity that put
them at risk HIV infection.  People who know what they're doing do not
include a class called "homosexual" or some variant thereon;  rather, they
include the class "mex who have sex with men", which is not the same
thing.  Lots of men who have sex with other men do not identify themselves
as homosexual, and if you ask the question the wrong way, you get the
wrong information.  This is especially true for certain ethnicities, at
least in the US. 

Another example from the AIDS biz is the term "sex worker" or "commercial
sex worker" instead of "prostitute" or more pejorative terms.  The special
purpose of these terms is to promote public health:  if you want to reach
the target audience, it's not a good move to start out by calling them by
a pejorative term.  It'd be like starting a message to statisticians with
"Hey geeks . . . ". 

Similarly, in the AIDS biz it is not uncommon to run across people of a
given sex, which denotes whether you have a Y chromosome, but a different
gender, which denotes the way you identify.  If you want to get the right
information, you have to ask the right question;  if you want to reach a
given audience, it is merely intelligent to address them accurately.

Thus, instead of seeing "sex vs. gender" as another example of English
debased by political rectitude, one might consider that such adaptations
are often pragmatic moves by people who are not grinding an axe but who
are trying to be effective at what they do. 

Jim Hodges

messages.subject: [S] Shocked and Puzzled
messages.body_plain:
Hi:                       

I use Watcom Fortran 77 Version 11.0 on my 600MHz Pentium III PC. While bench
marking its CPU time against an Alpha 266 MHz machine, I ended up in the
shocking news that my 600MHz (256MB RAM) Pentium III machine using Watcom
Version 11.0 is 66.4 times slower than the Alpha machine (the Alpha machine
takes 19 seconds while my Pentium needs 21 minutes to complete the job) . I
would appreciate it if you could send me any idea that will help the situation.
The compilation statements  and the fortran routine that I used are given
below:

Watcom compilation statements:

SET WFL386 = /P /4 /OR /OT /OM
SET FINCLUDE = C:\FORTRAN
WFL386 /L = DOS4G C:\FORTRAN/ %1 %2 %3 %4 %5
DOS4GW %

I also used the switches: /oneatx /zp4 /5r /fpi87 /fp5
but it got worse. 

c Fortran program used to bench mark

        do 1 i=1,9999999
        do 2 jj=1,100
        aj=float(i*2/(i*3)) +exp(-exp(sin(1.888)))
        b=atan((aj))+sin(3.1444440)
        c=sin(b)
2       continue
1       continue
        print*,jj,i,b,c
        stop
        end

Now the puzzle is that my Pentium was about 2.3  (Pentium takes 2062.6 seconds
while the Alpha machine needs 4843 seconds) times faster than the above Alpha
machine when I ran a Maple version of the program. The Maple routine is given
below:

# Maple program used for bench marking

        for i from 1 to 9999999 do
        for jj from 1 to 1 do
        j:=evalf(i*2/(i*3) +exp(-exp(sin(1.888))));
        b:=evalf(arctan((j))+sin(3.1444440));
        c:=evalf(sin(b));
        od;
        od;
        print(jj,i,b,c);

Thank you for help.

Sincerely yours,

M. Keramat Ali

messages.subject: [S] off-topic
messages.body_plain:
This is way off topic but there is a repository of knowledge on this 
list that may help me out of a problem.  Problem is that I pretty 
much have to exchange documents with research collaborators in 
a Word compatible format, and compatible means table, graphics 
and annotation/change tracking compatible.  I am also bound (less 
so) to the bibliographic software I use (EndNote) which is 
Mac/Windows and fairly user-friendly working as a Word add-in.

For my stats work I use site licenced copies of SAS 6.12 for 
Windows, SPSS (8.02?) and S+ (4.5 at present) plus a number of 
smaller packages for specialist work.  (I may move more to R for 
as much of this as I can ... if I can find the energy!)

Problem: Word97 and Win95 are losing communication. It only 
happens in documents with tables in, possibly only when there are 
tables and annotations/change tracking -- not sure.  It _may_ be 
that it only happens when the tables came from SPSS  but I'm not 
absolutely sure of this.  Once this starts happening to a file it's as 
if the file is seriously corrupted.  Sometimes saving to RTF (if I can) 
and reloading seems to help, sometimes  it doesn't.  This has 
reappeared after a complete rebuild of Win95 and reinstallation of 
Word97 and seems to happen under NT (4.1sp3) as well. The 
problem is approaching the point where I down tools and tech 
support available to me isn't solving it.

I am so furious and desperate I want to change.  I can't change 
hardware (no pennies), I'd love to change to linux and R and LaTeX 
or the like but that's a hell of learning curve, cuts me off from a 
huge repository of Email in my Email client, from my bibliographic 
s'ware and, _FATAL_ this!, from my collaborators.  

I have three questions:
1) anyone else recognise this problem and have a solution?
2) anyone think it goes away with Win98?
3) anyone got experience of StarOffice under linux and Word97 
comptability at the level of tables, graphics and annotation/change

messages.subject: Re: [S] Sex/Gender
messages.body_plain:
I realize this is not a core topic for s-news but it is important in
survey statistics.  Just a few points:

(1) I think Adrian Baddeley is right about why social scientists started
using the term "gender".  Unfortunately, they did not coin a new term but
took one from linguistics.  In language, there are three genders,
masculine, feminine, and neuter.  For example, in Spanish a table is the
feminine gender.  In German boys and girls are the neuter gender.

(2) Many people who fill out questionnaires don't know what "gender" is
supposed to mean.  This is certainly more of a problem than putting "yes"
or "no" for "sex" (which couldn't be done on most forms).  

(3) In the United States, "sex" is still the term used on U.S Government
surveys.  (At my agency, it was recently decided that one can use either
term in a report so long as one is consistent.)

Here are some points in favor of "gender":

(1) As both Adrian Baddeley and Jim Hodges have pointed out, a person's
(social) gender may be different from their (biological) sex.  Thus if one
wants the former, one needs a term for it.  It is not always clear to me
which one we really want though.

(2) The American Psychological Association (APA) requires "gender" in
their journals.  Many social science journals follow the APA style so it
saves rewriting to use "gender" in reports.

(3) "Sex" is sometimes used to mean "sexual intercourse" as in "having
sex".  So far, I haven't heard "having gender"!

Finally, it might seem one could get around the problem by simply asking
if the person is a man or a women.  But we are also intersted in boys and
girls and babies.  Male/female might work, but some people don't like
it...

___________________________________________________________________________
Michael P. Cohen                              phone 202-219-1917
National Center for Education Statistics      fax   202-219-1736
555 New Jersey Avenue NW #402            Internet mcohen at inet.ed.gov       
Washington DC 20208-5654 USA
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

On Mon, 11 Oct 1999, Adrian Baddeley wrote:

> 
> 
> A social scientist told me that 'gender' was coined
> to signify the "sex" which a person identifies with, as opposed to
> their actual biological sex (according to their DNA, say). 
> 
> So a male-to-female transsexual would have Sex=M and Gender=F. 
> Also, rarely, abnormal foetal or childhood development leads to a person
> appearing to be of one sex but being genetically of another sex.
> 
> Only social scientists are sophisticated enough to hold this
> distinction clear in their minds. Everyone else has simply
> substituted "Gender" for "Sex" throughout.
> Leading to news-clippings like:
> 
>       "Bruce can determine the gender of a newly-hatched chicken
>                in 15 seconds"
> 
>       "Risk factors for decompression sickness include age, overweight, 
>               and female gender. To reduce your risk of DCS it's important
>               to maintain your fitness. Of course you can't do anything
>               about your age or your gender"
> 
> 
> Mostly I dislike the advent of "gender" because it ruined a 
> good joke about statisticians!
> 
> ----
> Prof Adrian Baddeley, Mathematics & Statistics, University of Western 
> Australia

Date: Wed, 28 Oct 1998 16:45:02 +0100
MIME-Version: 1.0
X-Mailer: Internet Mail Service (5.0.1460.8)
Content-Type: text/plain
Sender: owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu <mailto:owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu>

Precedence: bulk

Hello again,

thanks for the quick reply concerning my query about
CIs for the median.

Brian Ripley points out the the "Hinge" is a definition
by Tukey, which is more-or-less the quartile (which itself
is not quite fully described). The correct definition should 
be in the EDA book by Tukey.
Any difference between the "Hinges" and Quartiles
should be small, except in small samples.

Luc Wouters (wouters at janbe.jnj.com <mailto:wouters at janbe.jnj.com> ) sent me
the following
function:

----------Message from Luc Wouters-------------------------
A distribution-free confidence interval on the median assuming only iid is
based on the order statistics and the binomial distribution. See Lehmann
(Nonparametrics: Statistical Methods Based on Ranks, Holden-Day, 1975, p.
182-183). The following S-Plus function can be used to set up such a 95 %
distribution-free confidence interval on the median:
"conf.med"<-function(x)
{
        v <- sort(x, na.last = NA)
        n <- length(x)
        if(n > 0) {
                m <- median(x)
                i <- qbinom(0.025, n, 0.5)
                if(i > 0)
                        r <- c(m, v[i], v[n - i + 1])
                else r <- c(m, NA, NA)
        }
        else r <- c(NA, NA, NA)
        r <- as.data.frame(list(median = r[1], lower = r[2], upper = r[3]))
        class(r) <- "table"
        r
}

conf.med(1:6)
>$median:
>[1] 3.5
>$lower:
>[1] 1
>$upper:
>[1] 6

Notice that a 95 % confidence interval can be obtained only when n > 5:

conf.med(1:5)
>$median:
>[1] 3
>$lower:
>[1] NA
>$upper:
>[1] NA

When the data are differences, then these C.I.'s are related to the sign
test. Notice that these C.I. have the disadvantage of being rather
conservative.
--------------------End of Message from Luc Wouters---------------------

Finally, answering my question whether there are better ways to do this,
Brian Ripley points out that robust estimators (available in S-PLUS)
might usually do a much better job than the median. A bootstrap approach
would then give probably better CIs for such estimators.

Thanks to all for helping me out on this.

Marcel

------------------------------------------------------------------------
Follow-up message from Scott Chasalow:
I have an SPLUS function for computing C.I.'s for any quantile, based
on the same ideas as is Luc Wouter's function.  Luc's function gives an
approximately symmetric 95% CI for the median.  Besides giving C.I.'s for
other
quantiles and for a specified range of coverage probabilities, I allow the 
user tocompute many different confidence intervals, perhaps with only
slightly 
different
coverage probabilities, different lengths, symmetric or not, and so on.  You
can
then look at them all and pick the one you prefer; the function can sort
them or
subset them in various ways to help you do so.
If anyone would like a copy of this function, please drop me an email.  The 
code,
including that for three local support functions,  is too long to send to

You can compute the confidence interval for median in various ways. You have
to write the program yourself. For large samples, median is distributed as
normal with mean sample median m and variance 1/4nf(m)^2, where f(m) is the
density at m. You can use a density estimator for estimating density at m.
However, you can also use bootstrap to compute percentile CI for median.
You can also see V&R (page 142).

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 12 Oct 1999, Jarrett J. Barber wrote:

> 
> I'm looking to use the Splus (version 3.4) function .Fortran() to call a
> 
> Fortran 90/95 object file.  I'm running SunOS 5.6.  The model of machine
> 
> is likely an Ultra 2 or Ultra 10, but I'm not sure (I connect via
> modem.).  The Fortran source file was compiled with NAGs Fortran 95 v
> 1.0 compiler using the following at the shell prompt:
> 
> f95 lvgram.f95 -c -o lvgram.o
> 
> At this point, as I understand it, I can use the dyn.load() function
> within Splus so I can then use the .Fortran() function.  However, I get
> the following error/messages.  Any suggestions?  Keep in mind that I'm a
> 
> novice Fortran programmer.  Also note that when I re-write and compile
> my subroutine in F77, the whole procedure works fine. However, I'd
> rather used Fortran90/95 for its added convenience and functionality
> (I'm even less proficient in F77.)
> 
> Thanks.
> 
> Jarrett Barber
> 
> In Splus:
> 
> > dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> Error in dyn.load("lvgram.o"): no definition for 7 symbols
> In addition: There were 7 warnings (use warnings() to see them)
> Dumped
> > warnings()
> Warning messages --
> 1: Undefined symbol: _F90FREE in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> 2: Undefined symbol: _HTON in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> 3: Undefined symbol: _F90ALLOC in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> 4: Undefined symbol: _F90_STOP in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> 5: Undefined symbol: _SUM0_S4 in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> 6: Undefined symbol: _F90_FCD_COPY in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> 7: Undefined symbol: _F90_FCD_BLANK in: dyn.load("lvgram.o")
> >

You have some missing library objects. This happens quite often with
Fortran loaded into S-PLUS this way. The simplest solution is probably
to used dyn.load.shared.  At a guess (I don't have that exact compiler:
-G is the flag to make a shared library in Solaris)

f95 -G -o lvgram.so lvgram.f95

then in S-PLUS

dyn.load.shared("./lvgram.so")

This has the advantage of being the route used by S-PLUS 5.x, of you
ever change over.

messages.subject: [S] Asking the right question
messages.body_plain:
In the Gender vs. Sex discussion, Jim Hodges wrote:

|> Similarly, in the AIDS biz it is not uncommon to run across people of a
|> given sex, which denotes whether you have a Y chromosome, but a different
|> gender, which denotes the way you identify.  If you want to get the right
|> information, you have to ask the right question;  if you want to reach a
|> given audience, it is merely intelligent to address them accurately.

Now there's another can of worms!  Whose version of "the right question"?

|> Thus, instead of seeing "sex vs. gender" as another example of English
|> debased by political rectitude, one might consider that such adaptations
|> are often pragmatic moves by people who are not grinding an axe but who
|> are trying to be effective at what they do. 

As with political rectitude in general, the motivation behind the
"pragmatic moves" is laudible, but the other implications of the
method chosen are usually ignored.

It brings to mind a Sample Surveys course I did at universtiy a few
years ago.  One of the "tablets of stone" we received from the
Sociology Department was engraved with the instructions that it was
inappropriate to ask in a survey the demographic question: 'What is
the source of your income?'  Because there are people who won't know
what those words mean, it was decreed that *the* way to ask the
question is: 'Where do you get your money from?'  IMHO, that question
is open to more misinterpretation than the one that it is claimed to
be superior to.

best

Patrick

messages.subject: [S] bioequivalence in S-Plus
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus Users,

this question is concerned with the statistical methodology for
assessment of population and individual bioequivalence (be)
on the basis of replicated and nonreplicated crossover designs.

The focus of these methods is especially on the estimation of the
(log-transformed) be measures (AUC, Cmax) and 
(i) the estimation of the total variance for each of the two formulations 
(population be), 
(ii) the subject-by-formulation interaction variance and within-subject 
variance (individual be),
(iii) the construction of confidence intervals for the above mentioned
criterions.

I'm just trying to implement these methods in S-Plus. I think using linear
mixed effects models and/or glm methods is the right way to do this, but
I'm especially not sure with point (iii) in this context.

Maybe anyone has already some experiences with this topic? Any help and
suggestions could be very useful.

I'm using S-Plus 2000 for Windows/NT.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Contrasts
messages.body_plain:
> 
> Dear Splus users,
> 
> Is there a way creating/retrieving a contrast matrix from a factor using
> built in function such as contr.helmert, contr.sum.
> For example, what I want if I use contr.sum:
> 
> Factor       Matrix
> 0                1    0
> 1                0    1
> 2               -1   -1
> 0                1    0
> 1                0    1
> 2               -1   -1
> 
> Thanks in advance.

Sure.  Here are two.  First the slightly obscure way:

> f <- factor(rep(0:2, 2))

> contr.sum(length(levels(f)))[f, ]
  [,1] [,2] 
1    1    0
2    0    1
3   -1   -1
1    1    0
2    0    1
3   -1   -1

This uses the fact that the contrast functions like contr.sum produce a
contrast matrix and the model matrix (section) is obtained by choosing rows
from it according to the factor.  This is not as well known as it should be.

Secondly, you can simply use the same tools that the model fitting functions
do.  

> g <- C(f, "contr.sum")

> model.matrix(~g)[, -1]
  g1 g2 
1  1  0
2  0  1
3 -1 -1
4  1  0
5  0  1
6 -1 -1

The [, -1] is to remove the intercept column.  The effect is quite different 
if you try to remove it in the formula (using ~ g - 1 say) as you could check.

Bill Venables.

(Please Note: No sex or gender this time...)

messages.subject: [S] generating correlated beta variates
messages.body_plain:
I searched the S-News archive and did not find a suggestion for my situation.  
I'd like to generate bivariate beta random variables with specified 
correlation.  Much has been discussed on S-News recently regarding correlated 
binary and normal variates, but have not seen anything on correlated beta 
variates.  Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

What I plan to do with these variates:

The kappa statistic for inter-rater agreement 'seems' to behave poorly when the 
objects being rated are not uniformly distributed across the entire scoring 
scale.  E.g., suppose a 4-point scale (0-3) is used, but 75% of the objects are 
scored 3, 24% scored 2, .5% each at 0 and 1.  Even though there is high 
agreement between the two raters (80% of objects are on diagonal), the observed 
kappa was 0.30.  I am interested in understanding the behavior of kappa in such 
non-uniform situations.  The plan is to generate bivariate beta scores as 
latent variables with specified correlation, collapse to categorical scores, 
and assess how observed kappa relates to correlation of the latent variates. 

In a series of papers by Cicchetti and Feinstein, they discuss paradoxes of 
kappa statistics in the context of 2-point scoring (yes/no; pos/neg).  They 
discuss the effect of prevalence on the kappa statistics and how severity of 
prevalence is related to the maximum possible kappa value that could be 
attained.  They propose adjusting the computed kappa by weighting by the 
maximum possible.  [To me, this indicates that kappa statistics should not be 
reviewed in isolation, but with some measure of observed prevalence.]  I am 
looking for an extension of Cicchetti and Feinstein's work to polytomous 
scales, and would appreciate any help on that as well.

Will summarize to the group.

Regards,

James Pratt
Sonus Pharmaceuticals
jimp at sonuspharma.com

messages.subject: [S] RE: Contrasts
messages.body_plain:
My sincere thanks to Brian Ripley, Bill Venables and Alan Zaslavsky for
their quick replies. My question and their answers are provided below.

Original question:
 
> Dear Splus users,
> 
> Is there a way creating/retrieving a contrast matrix from a factor using
> built in function such as contr.helmert, contr.sum.
> For example, what I want if I use contr.sum:
> 
> Factor       Matrix
> 0                1    0
> 1                0    1
> 2               -1   -1
> 0                1    0
> 1                0    1
> 2               -1   -1
--------------------------------------

Brian Ripley:

There are several ways:

z <- factor(c(0:2, 0:2))
zz <- attr(C(z, sum), "contrasts")
zz[z, ]
  [,1] [,2] 
0    1    0
1    0    1
2   -1   -1
0    1    0
1    0    1
2   -1   -1

is one of the simplest.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Bill Venables:

Sure.  Here are two.  First the slightly obscure way:

> f <- factor(rep(0:2, 2))

> contr.sum(length(levels(f)))[f, ]
  [,1] [,2] 
1    1    0
2    0    1
3   -1   -1
1    1    0
2    0    1
3   -1   -1

This uses the fact that the contrast functions like contr.sum produce a
contrast matrix and the model matrix (section) is obtained by choosing rows
from it according to the factor.  This is not as well known as it should be.

Secondly, you can simply use the same tools that the model fitting functions
do.  

> g <- C(f, "contr.sum")

> model.matrix(~g)[, -1]
  g1 g2 
1  1  0
2  0  1
3 -1 -1
4  1  0
5  0  1
6 -1 -1

The [, -1] is to remove the intercept column.  The effect is quite different

if you try to remove it in the formula (using ~ g - 1 say) as you could
check.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
-

Alan Zaslavsky:

contr.helmert(my.factor)[my.factor,]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
